title: Curtain Call for Tako: The Piano-Playing Octopus Retires
summary:
The world's most unlikely musician has hung up his tentacles. Tako, the piano-playing octopus, has officially retired, according to his owner, Swedish YouTuber Mattias Krantz.

Krantz had a wild dream: teach an animal to play the piano. In March 2025, he picked an octopus from a fish market and named him Takoyaki, or Tako for short. 'I've always wanted to teach an animal piano,' Krantz explained. 'In theory, octopuses have incredible potential. They're as smart as a three-year-old, amazing problem-solvers, and each of their eight arms has its own mini brain. It's like having eight pianists in one body.'

But octopuses are not natural pianists. They can't hear airborne sounds, so Krantz installed a vibrating speaker in the tank so Tako could feel the music. They also prefer pulling to pushing, so Krantz built a custom keyboard with pull-keys. And to motivate his student, he rigged a 'crab elevator' that lowered a live crab into the tank whenever Tako hit the right notes. Talk about positive reinforcement!

For six months, Krantz trained Tako through trial and error, documenting the process on YouTube. There were moments he almost gave up. But finally, Tako learned to play sequences of notes. The breakthrough was captured in a documentary released on November 5, 2025, showing Tako pulling keys alongside Krantz's guitar. The video went viral, making Tako an internet sensation.

Unfortunately, octopuses have short lifespans, and Tako is now in his final stage of life, naturally losing energy and sleeping more. Rather than push for more content, Krantz turned off the cameras to let his friend enjoy a peaceful retirement in his favorite tank cave. It's a bittersweet ending, but Tako earned his rest—and proved that even a creature with no bones can rock out.
why_it_matters: Tako's retirement raises broader questions about the ethics of animal entertainment: how much should humans ask of intelligent creatures, and when should cameras stop rolling? It also shows that animal intelligence can surprise us, but that scientific and social curiosity must be balanced with care and respect for an animal's natural limits.

background_read: Octopuses are widely considered among the most intelligent invertebrates on Earth; they can solve mazes, open jars, and use tools, and their arms contain a dense network of neurons that allows each arm to move somewhat independently.
Most octopus species have short lives, with many common octopuses living roughly one to two years, so a six-month training project can take up a large share of an adult octopus's life.
Unlike humans, octopuses cannot hear airborne sounds well; they sense vibrations through the water around them, which presented a major technical challenge for the piano project.
Mattias Krantz (a Swedish YouTuber known for engineering and technology videos) treated the project as an unusual engineering puzzle and documented it on his channel for a wide online audience.

Animal trainers often use positive reinforcement—rewarding a desired action with food—and Krantz adapted that idea by building a 'crab elevator' that delivered a live crab when Tako pulled the correct keys.

perspectives.description: For Krantz, Tako's ability to learn sequences was a triumph of creativity and patience, proving that an octopus could produce something musical. Many viewers saw it as a heartwarming story and a window into animal intelligence.

Critics might argue that keeping an octopus in a tank and training it with live crab rewards is stressful or ethically risky, especially since octopuses have short lives. The decision to stop filming only at the final stage could be seen as too late for Tako's well-being.

From a scientific angle, the project was less about piano playing and more about testing how an octopus can solve a novel problem under human-designed conditions. The training success does not necessarily mean Tako understood music; it shows operant conditioning and adaptation.

Future animal-training projects might build welfare limits into the design from the start, rather than retiring an animal only when it becomes visibly tired. Tako's story could encourage clearer rules for using intelligent animals in online content and research.
